initial_requirements: NJIT needs a secure distance-learning environment that helps professors communicate and work with students online. Virtual-EDU should provide a classroom-like portal where enrolled users can communicate individually or in groups, share and collaborate on learning materials, and participate in online course activities. Administrators will also need to manage the learning environment and its enrolled users.
finish_message: SparkMe interview completed (agenda completed or max turns reached).

messages.content: Hi, thanks so much for taking the time to chat today. I'm looking forward to hearing more about Virtual-EDU and how it can best support NJIT's distance-learning needs. The way this will go is pretty simple: I'll ask you some questions, but feel free to pause or ask me to clarify anything at any point. To get started, could you describe the project context and the problem the system should address from your perspective?

Virtual-EDU is meant to give NJIT a secure online learning space that feels close to a real classroom when people can’t be on campus. Right now the main problem is that professors and students need a reliable way to communicate, share course materials, work together, and handle class activities without everything being spread across separate tools. The system should bring those interactions into one place while still giving administrators control over access and the overall environment.

Thanks for that overview! To get a clearer picture, could you share what the main goals NJIT hopes to achieve with Virtual-EDU? For example, are there specific improvements or capabilities the system should deliver to make distance learning more effective or efficient?

The main goal is to make distance learning feel organized, secure, and easy to use for both instructors and students. NJIT wants professors to be able to post materials, run discussions, give assignments, and communicate with students without a lot of friction, while students should be able to access everything from one place and collaborate with classmates. It should also reduce administrative overhead by giving staff better control over users, courses, and access.

That makes a lot of sense—having everything streamlined and secure is definitely key. To help us understand success a bit better, could you share what measurable outcomes NJIT hopes to see from Virtual-EDU? For example, are there specific improvements in student engagement, professor productivity, or administrative efficiency that you’d like to track?

I think NJIT would want to see higher student participation in class discussions and course activities, along with fewer missed communications because everything is in one system. For professors, success would look like less time spent juggling tools and easier delivery of materials, assignments, and feedback. On the administrative side, better control over enrollments and fewer support issues would be the main efficiency gains.

Thanks for sharing those outcomes—it really helps to understand what success looks like. To get a clearer picture of who will be using Virtual-EDU, could you walk me through the main stakeholder roles involved? For example, who are the key users or groups, and what are their primary responsibilities or interactions with the system?

The main groups are students, professors, and administrators. Students will mainly access course content, submit work, join discussions, and communicate with instructors or classmates, while professors will manage their classes, post materials, create activities, and evaluate student work. Administrators will handle user accounts, course access, and overall system oversight, and I’m not sure yet whether there will be any special support roles beyond that.

Can you describe the current work situation for professors, students, and administrators regarding distance learning? Specifically, what tools are they using now, and what challenges do they encounter in their daily activities?

Right now, it’s pretty fragmented, with people often relying on a mix of email, shared drives, chat tools, and separate video meeting platforms. That creates problems because course materials, discussions, and assignments are scattered, so it’s easy for students to miss things and for professors to spend too much time coordinating across different systems. Administrators also have a harder time keeping track of users and access when everything isn’t centralized.

Thanks for that overview of the current tool situation. Could you walk me through a typical day or week for professors, students, and administrators as they manage their distance learning tasks? For example, what steps do they take to share materials, communicate, or handle assignments, and where do they usually run into the biggest frustrations or delays?

A professor usually starts by posting lecture materials or announcements, then answers student emails or messages throughout the day, and later collects assignments and gives feedback. Students check for updates, download materials, ask questions, and submit their work, often having to jump between tools to figure out what’s due. Administrators spend a lot of time enrolling users, fixing access problems, and making sure classes and accounts are set up correctly, and the biggest delays usually come from manual coordination and people not knowing where to find the latest information.

Thanks for that detailed look at daily activities and challenges. To get a better sense of how Virtual-EDU needs to support NJIT’s rhythms, could you describe the key academic or administrative business events—like enrollment periods, exam weeks, or grading deadlines—that the system must handle effectively? How do these events typically impact how professors, students, and administrators use the system?

The biggest peaks are the start of a term, when students are enrolling and classes are being set up, and then midterms and finals, when assignment submission, discussions, and grading activity all spike. During those periods, professors need the system to stay reliable and easy to update, students need quick access to materials and deadlines, and administrators are usually dealing with account changes and access issues. I’d also say grading deadlines and add/drop periods matter because they create a lot of last-minute coordination and support requests.

That’s really helpful to understand the busy times and their impact. To get a clearer picture of day-to-day use, could you walk me through the typical workflows professors, students, and administrators follow during a normal week? For example, what are the main steps they take to share materials, communicate, or manage assignments, and where do they usually hit the biggest pain points or delays?

A normal week for a professor is usually posting the week’s materials, sending announcements, replying to questions, and reviewing submissions as they come in. Students check the portal for updates, download what they need, ask questions, and turn in assignments, but they can lose time if deadlines or files are hard to find. Administrators mostly monitor enrollments, resolve access problems, and help keep the classes organized, and the main pain points are usually manual updates, duplicated communication, and support requests about missing or incorrect access.

That gives a clear picture of their weekly routines and challenges. To make sure Virtual-EDU really supports them well, could you describe the specific functions or features the system should provide for professors, students, and administrators? For example, what capabilities would help reduce their biggest frustrations or make their tasks easier and more efficient?

For professors, the system should make it easy to post materials, send announcements, manage assignments, grade work, and communicate with individuals or groups in one place. For students, it should provide a simple way to find course content, participate in discussions, submit assignments, and get timely feedback or notifications. For administrators, the key features are user and course management, access control, and tools for monitoring the platform so they can resolve issues quickly and keep everything organized.

You’ve outlined some great features for each user group. To make sure the system supports their workflows properly, could you describe any specific business rules or policies Virtual-EDU should enforce? For example, rules about who can access or modify materials, deadlines for assignments, communication protocols, or any other guidelines that help keep things running smoothly and fairly?

Yes, the system should enforce role-based access so students can only see the courses they’re enrolled in, and professors can only manage their own classes unless an administrator grants broader access. Assignment deadlines should be controlled by the course setup, and after a deadline the system should either block submissions or only allow late submissions if the professor has enabled that policy. Communication should stay within the class or approved group context, and I believe administrators should be able to override access or account settings when needed, but the exact policy details would need to be confirmed with NJIT.

That’s a solid foundation for the system’s business rules. To build on that, are there any mandated solution constraints NJIT requires us to follow? For example, specific security standards, data retention policies, integration requirements with other systems, or any technical or organizational rules that Virtual-EDU must comply with?

Security is definitely a major constraint, since this system will hold student and course information, so it needs strong authentication, access control, and protection for data in transit and at rest. I also expect it will need to fit into NJIT’s existing identity and user-management setup, and probably work with whatever student information or enrollment systems are already in place. I’m not sure yet about the exact retention policy or required standards, so that would need to be verified with the university.

Since we touched on security and integration, I’m curious about how Virtual-EDU should handle the lifecycle of key data like course materials, assignments, and communications. Could you walk me through what happens from when these items are created, updated, maybe archived, or even deleted? How should the system manage this over time to keep things organized and compliant?

Course materials and assignments would usually be created by the professor, updated as needed during the term, and then kept available to enrolled users until the course ends. After the term, I’d expect the system to archive the course content and records so they can still be referenced later if needed, but I’m not sure how long NJIT wants to keep them before deletion. Messages and submissions probably need to be retained for a defined period for academic or compliance reasons, so those rules should be tied to university policy rather than left to individual users.

Could you describe how Virtual-EDU should handle archiving and retrieval of course materials, assignments, and communications after a term ends? For example, who can access archived data, how long it should be kept, and what processes should be in place for eventual deletion or compliance with retention policies?

After a term ends, archived course data should still be accessible to the professor, the students who were enrolled, and administrators, but only through controlled access rather than regular class editing. I don’t know the exact retention period NJIT wants, so that would need to be set by policy, but the system should support keeping records for as long as required and then deleting them in a way that is secure and auditable. If there are legal or compliance holds, those records should be preserved until the hold is lifted, even if the normal retention period has expired.

Thanks for clarifying the archiving and access controls after a term ends. To help us design the system’s data structure well, could you describe in detail the key data entities Virtual-EDU will manage? For example, course materials, assignments, users, communications, and so on. What specific attributes or metadata should the system track for each to support the platform’s functionality effectively?

The core entities should include users, courses, enrollments, materials, assignments, submissions, grades, and communications. For users, the system should track identity details, role, contact info, and account status; for courses, things like course code, title, term, instructor, and enrolled roster; for materials and assignments, titles, descriptions, due dates, ownership, versioning, and visibility; and for communications, sender, recipients, timestamps, course or group association, and message status. Submissions and grades should also keep timestamps, file references, feedback, and any late or resubmission indicators so the history is clear.

That’s a great overview of the core data entities and their key attributes. To help us design the data model more precisely, could you share if there are any important relationships or dependencies between these entities we should be aware of? For example, how materials link to assignments or courses, how submissions relate to assignments and students, or any special rules about versioning or visibility that affect these data connections?

Yes, the main dependency is that everything should hang off the course, since materials, assignments, and communications are typically course-specific. Assignments belong to one course, submissions belong to one assignment and one student, and grades belong to a submission, with the professor as the grader. Visibility should follow enrollment and role, so students only see items tied to their active course access, while versioning matters for materials and assignments because updates should not overwrite the history in a way that loses what was actually published at the time.

Thanks for explaining those relationships and visibility rules clearly. To help us design the data model precisely, could you describe in more detail the key data entities Virtual-EDU will manage—like users, courses, materials, assignments, communications, and so on? Specifically, what attributes or metadata should the system track for each to support the platform’s functionality effectively?

Sure. For users, I’d expect the system to track a unique ID, name, email, role, department or program if relevant, account status, and authentication info tied to NJIT’s login process. For courses, it should store course ID, course code, title, term, section, instructor, enrollment status, and archived state. For materials and assignments, useful metadata would be title, description, owner, creation and update timestamps, visibility, due date for assignments, attached files or links, and version history. For communications, it should keep sender, recipients, course or group association, timestamp, content or attachment references, and whether the message was read or replied to.

You’ve given a solid overview of the key data entities and their attributes. Shifting gears a bit, could you share any project delivery constraints or policies NJIT expects Virtual-EDU to follow? For example, are there specific rules about how long data must be retained, how deletion should be handled, or any audit requirements to ensure compliance during the system’s operation?

I know NJIT would expect the system to support retention and deletion rules that can be adjusted by policy, because those requirements may differ by record type. Deletion should be controlled and auditable, meaning we need to know who deleted what, when, and under what authority, and some data may need to be preserved if there’s a compliance hold. I’m not sure of the exact retention periods or audit depth yet, so those would need to come from the university’s policy and legal teams.

That makes sense about needing flexible, policy-driven retention and auditable deletion with compliance holds. To help us plan the system’s audit and compliance features, could you describe what kinds of audit trails or logs NJIT expects? For example, should the system track just deletions and data changes, or also user access, login attempts, and communication activities? And are there any specific reporting or alerting needs tied to these audit records?

Yes, I’d expect the audit trail to cover more than just deletions and data changes. It should also record logins and failed login attempts, role or permission changes, access to sensitive course data, file downloads or uploads, and key communication actions like posting, editing, or deleting messages. For reporting, administrators would likely need searchable logs and some kind of export for investigations or compliance reviews, and it would be useful to have alerts for suspicious access patterns or repeated failed authentication attempts.

That’s very helpful detail on the audit trail scope and reporting needs. To make sure we cover all security angles, could you describe any specific requirements or expectations NJIT has around system availability and reliability? For example, how critical is uptime during peak periods like term start or grading deadlines, and what level of fault tolerance or backup should Virtual-EDU provide to avoid disruptions?

Virtual-EDU should be highly available during peak academic periods, especially at term start, exam time, and grading deadlines, because disruptions there would affect a lot of people at once. I’d expect routine backups, disaster recovery capability, and fault tolerance so that a single server or component failure doesn’t take the whole platform down. I don’t know the exact uptime target NJIT would mandate, but the system should clearly prioritize continuity and quick recovery.

Since accessibility is so important for an educational platform, could you share how Virtual-EDU should ensure that all users—including those with disabilities—can effectively access and use core features like course materials, communications, and assignments? Are there specific accessibility standards or accommodations NJIT expects the system to support?

Virtual-EDU should be usable with screen readers, keyboard-only navigation, good color contrast, and captions or transcripts for any audio or video content. I’d also expect accessible document handling for materials and assignments, so uploaded files and forms don’t create barriers for students or faculty. I’m not sure which exact standard NJIT wants to cite, but it would be safest to align with common higher-ed accessibility expectations and make accommodations configurable where possible.

That’s a great foundation for accessibility. Building on that, how does NJIT expect Virtual-EDU to verify and maintain accessibility over time? For example, are there specific testing processes, compliance certifications, or user feedback mechanisms the system should support to ensure ongoing accessibility?

I’d expect accessibility to be checked during development and again before major releases, with some kind of review or testing against the chosen standard. It would also help to have a way for users to report accessibility problems directly in the platform, so issues can be tracked and resolved instead of just informally reported. I’m not aware of any specific certification NJIT requires for this project, so that would need confirmation from the accessibility or compliance office.

That makes sense about testing and user feedback for accessibility. To get a clearer picture, could you describe what specific accessibility features or accommodations NJIT expects Virtual-EDU to provide? For example, how should the system handle navigation, content presentation, or interaction to ensure all users, including those with disabilities, can effectively access course materials, communications, and assignments?

It should support keyboard-only use throughout the main workflows, with menus, forms, assignments, and messaging all reachable without a mouse. Content should be presented in a clean, consistent way with readable text sizes, strong contrast, proper labels on controls, and support for captions, transcripts, and alternative text where media is involved. For interactions, error messages should be clear and tied to the relevant field, and I’d expect users to be able to adjust things like display preferences if that helps with accessibility.

You’ve shared great details on the accessibility features Virtual-EDU should provide. Looking ahead, how does NJIT envision maintaining and verifying accessibility over time? For instance, are there specific ongoing processes, roles, or tools the system should support to monitor compliance and handle user feedback on accessibility issues?

I’d expect accessibility to be treated as an ongoing operational responsibility, not just a one-time release check. The system should support periodic audits, issue tracking for accessibility defects, and a clear path for users to submit feedback or requests for accommodation. I’m not sure which team NJIT wants to own that process day to day, but the platform should make it easy for administrators to monitor problems and confirm they’ve been addressed.

Thanks for clarifying how accessibility should be managed continuously. Shifting gears a bit, could you describe NJIT’s expectations for Virtual-EDU’s capacity to handle peak loads—like at term start, midterms, and finals? How should the system manage spikes in simultaneous user activity during these critical academic periods?

Virtual-EDU should be able to handle heavy concurrency during those peak academic windows without slowing to a crawl or dropping sessions. I’d expect the system to scale up enough for a large number of simultaneous logins, file uploads, discussion posts, and assignment submissions, because those are exactly the times everyone is trying to use it at once. If the load gets unusually high, it should degrade gracefully rather than fail outright, and administrators should be able to see when capacity is getting tight.

That’s helpful to understand how Virtual-EDU should handle peak loads. Looking ahead, how does NJIT envision the platform scaling over time? For example, should it automatically adjust resources during unexpected surges or support growth in users and courses without manual intervention? Any particular scalability features or strategies NJIT expects?

Yes, ideally it should scale with growth in enrollment, course count, and usage without needing constant manual reconfiguration. Automatic resource adjustment during unexpected surges would be very valuable, especially around registration and deadline periods when usage can jump quickly. I’d also expect the design to avoid obvious bottlenecks so NJIT can add capacity over time without having to redesign the whole platform.

That’s great insight on scaling and avoiding bottlenecks. Shifting a bit, could you share how NJIT expects Virtual-EDU to handle response performance around submissions and grading? For example, how important is it to track timestamps, feedback delivery, and indicators for late or resubmissions to maintain a clear and reliable grading history?

That’s pretty important. The system should record timestamps for submissions, grading actions, and feedback so there’s a reliable audit trail, especially when deadlines or disputes come up. It should also clearly mark late work, resubmissions, and version history so professors and students can see exactly what was turned in and when.

You mentioned the importance of tracking timestamps and marking late or resubmissions clearly for grading history. Could you describe how timely feedback delivery should be handled in Virtual-EDU? For example, are there expectations for notifying students immediately when feedback is posted, or any specific workflows professors should follow to ensure feedback is both prompt and clear?

Yes, students should be notified when feedback is posted, ideally right away through the platform, and possibly by email as well if that’s enabled. I’d expect professors to be able to release feedback when they’re ready, either for the whole class or for individual students, and the workflow should make it clear whether grades are still provisional. The key expectation is that feedback is visible quickly, easy to find, and tied directly to the assignment or submission it refers to.

Now that we’ve covered feedback workflows, I’d like to ask about the transition to Virtual-EDU. Does NJIT expect to migrate existing course materials, user data, or communications from current tools into the new platform? If so, could you describe what kinds of data or content should be migrated and any key considerations or challenges you foresee in that migration process?

Yes, there should be migration support for at least the core course materials and user accounts, and possibly some historical course content depending on what NJIT decides to carry forward. Things like syllabi, documents, assignment descriptions, grades, and basic enrollment data are likely candidates, but I’m not sure whether old messages or discussion archives need to come over in every case. A big concern would be preserving structure and access permissions correctly, because the migrated data has to land in the right course spaces without exposing anything to the wrong users.

That makes a lot of sense, especially about preserving structure and access controls during migration. Could you share how NJIT envisions the actual migration process? For example, are there expectations around timing, automation, validation steps, or how to handle any issues that come up during migration?

I’d expect migration to be mostly automated where possible, with a structured cutover plan so it doesn’t interfere too much with the semester schedule. Validation is important, so NJIT would likely want checks to confirm files, enrollments, and permissions moved correctly before going live. If problems come up, the process should log them clearly and let administrators retry or correct specific items rather than failing the entire migration.

Thanks for explaining the migration process so clearly. To build on that, could you describe NJIT’s expectations around data conversion during migration? For example, are there specific file formats, metadata standards, or transformation rules that Virtual-EDU should support to ensure course materials and assignments import correctly and maintain integrity?

We’d want Virtual-EDU to handle the common academic file types without breaking them, like PDF, Word documents, spreadsheets, images, and standard video or audio formats if those are being used. Metadata is important too, especially course name, term, owner, due dates, and permission info, because that’s what keeps the content organized and usable after import. I don’t know that there’s a single NJIT-wide standard already decided for every source system, but the conversion should preserve as much original structure and context as possible and flag anything it can’t map cleanly.

Thanks for sharing those details on data formats and metadata. To get a fuller picture, could you describe NJIT’s overall plans or expectations for migrating existing course data and user information into Virtual-EDU? Are there particular challenges or priorities around the migration process that we should be aware of to ensure a smooth transition?

The main priority is a smooth transition with minimal disruption to active classes, so course data and user information need to come across accurately and on time. We’d want the migration to preserve identity relationships, enrollments, permissions, and key content so instructors don’t have to rebuild courses from scratch. The biggest challenges are usually data quality, mismatched formats between old tools and the new platform, and making sure nothing sensitive is exposed during the move.

Thanks for outlining those migration priorities and challenges. To help us design the migration process effectively, could you share more about NJIT’s expectations for automation and validation during migration? For example, how much manual intervention is acceptable, what kinds of validation checks are critical before going live, and how should errors or mismatches be handled to minimize disruption?

We’d want as much of the migration as possible to be automated so staff aren’t spending a lot of time doing manual cleanup. Manual intervention should really be limited to exceptions, like bad source data, ambiguous mappings, or anything that fails validation. Before going live, the critical checks are that users are matched correctly, enrollments and permissions are right, course materials open properly, and no content or grades were lost or duplicated. If there are errors or mismatches, they should be reported clearly, queued for review, and fixable in a targeted way without restarting the entire migration.

To understand how Virtual-EDU should support grading and feedback, could you describe NJIT’s expectations for timely feedback delivery workflows? For example, what key steps should professors follow to release feedback, and how should students be notified to ensure they become promptly aware and clearly understand their results?

Professors should be able to enter feedback, review it, and then explicitly publish or release it when they’re ready. Once it’s released, students should get a clear notification inside the platform, and ideally an email alert too if that’s part of the setup. The feedback view should make it obvious which assignment it belongs to, whether the grade is final or still provisional, and any comments or rubric details should be easy for students to understand.

That sounds like a solid approach to feedback release and notification. To get a clearer picture, could you walk me through the typical workflow professors would follow from entering feedback to publishing it? For example, are there any review or approval steps, options to release feedback in batches or individually, or ways to handle provisional grades? Also, how should the system handle notifications to ensure students don’t miss important updates?

Typically, the professor would enter grades and comments, save them as draft or provisional, and then do a final review before publishing. We’d want support for releasing feedback either one student at a time or in batches for the whole class, since both patterns happen depending on the assignment. For provisional grades, the system should clearly label them as not final and avoid triggering the same level of notification as a confirmed release unless the professor intends that.

That’s very helpful detail on the feedback workflow and provisional grades. To make sure students don’t miss important feedback, how does NJIT envision the notification process working? For example, should the system send reminders or escalate alerts if students don’t view their feedback within a certain timeframe? Are there preferred channels or timing for these notifications to keep students promptly informed without overwhelming them?

We’d want the initial notification to go out right when feedback is released, and that should be enough in most cases. Email and an in-system alert are the main channels I’d expect, but I’m not sure NJIT would want a lot of escalation beyond that unless it’s for something urgent like a deadline or a required correction. Reminders could be useful, but they should be configurable so we don’t end up spamming students for every grade update.

Thanks for clarifying the notification preferences. To help us anticipate potential challenges, have there been any past or anticipated situations where requirements around feedback release timing, notification frequency, or privacy created conflicts or trade-offs for NJIT? For example, balancing timely alerts with avoiding notification overload or managing provisional versus final grades?

Yes, that balance is definitely a concern. Professors want students to see updates quickly, but too many alerts can become noise, especially in courses with lots of small assignments. Privacy is the other issue, since provisional grades or sensitive feedback shouldn’t be exposed too broadly, so we’d need controls that let instructors choose what gets released, to whom, and when.

It’s great to hear about the need for flexible controls to balance timely feedback and privacy. Could you share any specific examples or scenarios where NJIT has faced or anticipates conflicts between releasing feedback quickly and protecting sensitive information? For instance, how have professors or administrators handled situations where provisional grades or sensitive comments needed careful timing or selective visibility?

A common case is when a professor has grades ready but wants to hold them until after the whole class has been reviewed, so nobody sees partial results too early. Another situation is when comments include sensitive academic concerns, and those need to stay visible only to the student and instructor, not in any broader class view. In those cases, the expectation is that the system supports selective release and clear visibility settings so instructors can control exactly when and how the information appears.

Thanks for those examples—they really highlight the need for precise control over feedback visibility. Could you share any specific situations NJIT has encountered where the timing or selective release of feedback led to conflicts or challenges? For instance, how have professors or administrators managed cases where releasing partial grades early caused issues, or where sensitive comments needed extra protection? Understanding these real-world scenarios will help us design better support for those trade-offs.

One challenge is when some students get feedback early because their work was graded first, and others notice the difference and think the instructor is favoring certain people. That usually pushes professors to wait and release everything together, or at least keep draft statuses hidden until the full set is ready. For sensitive comments, the main concern is accidental exposure through class lists, shared views, or notifications, so the system needs very tight per-student visibility and confirmation before anything is published.

Could you describe specific examples or scenarios where NJIT has experienced conflicts between the need to release feedback quickly and the need to protect sensitive or provisional information? How have professors or administrators managed these situations so far?

A typical example is when an instructor finishes grading a subset of submissions early, but wants to wait because the comments include corrections or concerns that should be handled consistently across the whole class. In practice, they usually keep everything in draft until the full review is done, then release it all at once to avoid confusion and complaints. For anything sensitive, the professor may share it directly with the individual student and avoid putting it in any broader announcement or class-visible context.

That makes sense, especially the need to keep draft feedback hidden until everything is ready. Looking ahead, are there any open issues or unresolved questions at NJIT about how to balance notification frequency with privacy controls? For example, are there any policy or technical uncertainties that might affect how these features get prioritized or implemented in Virtual-EDU?

Yes, there are still some open questions around how much control instructors should have versus how much should be standardized for consistency across courses. We also haven’t fully settled what counts as a required notification versus an optional reminder, especially when privacy is involved and we don’t want repeated alerts exposing too much detail. I’d say the policy side is still being worked out, so that could affect whether the system leans toward simple default behavior or more configurable options.

Given the open questions around notification frequency and privacy, could you describe how NJIT envisions escalation or reminder policies for feedback notifications? For example, should the system send repeated reminders if students don’t view feedback promptly, or escalate alerts to professors or administrators? How configurable should these policies be to balance timely awareness without causing notification fatigue?

I think the default should be one initial notification and maybe a single reminder after a reasonable delay, but not an aggressive chain of alerts. Escalating to professors or administrators would probably only make sense for truly time-sensitive items, not routine feedback, because that could create a lot of unnecessary overhead. Ideally, the reminder policy should be configurable at the course level or by instructors, with NJIT setting a broad standard so students aren’t flooded differently in every class.

That approach to a default plus configurable reminders sounds like a good balance. Could you describe how NJIT envisions the details of these escalation and reminder policies working? For example, what specific triggers should cause reminders to be sent, who should receive escalations if feedback remains unacknowledged, and how much flexibility should professors or administrators have to customize these settings within their courses?

A reminder should probably be triggered only after feedback has been posted and the student hasn’t opened it within a set window, maybe a day or two for ordinary items. If something is truly urgent, like a deadline-related correction or a required academic notice, then an escalation could go to the professor first, not straight to an administrator. Professors should have some flexibility to adjust timing within NJIT’s limits, but administrators would likely want guardrails so people can’t create constant alerts or hide important notices too long.

Thanks for outlining those key points on timing and escalation recipients. To get a clearer picture, could you walk me through how NJIT envisions these escalation and reminder policies working in practice? For example, what specific events or triggers should prompt reminders or escalations, who exactly should receive these alerts at each stage, and how much flexibility should professors or administrators have to customize these settings within their courses or roles?

In practice, I’d expect a reminder to go out when feedback is posted, then another only if it stays unread past a course-defined window, and only for items marked as important or time-sensitive. If it still isn’t acknowledged, the next alert would usually go to the professor or course staff, since they are the ones who can decide whether follow-up is needed. Professors should be able to tune the timing a bit for their courses, but NJIT would probably want administrators to set limits on minimum and maximum delays, plus what kinds of messages are allowed to escalate at all.

Building on what you shared about escalation policies, could you describe how NJIT currently handles situations where students repeatedly ignore feedback notifications? Are there any manual or automated escalation steps in place, and how well have those worked so far?

Right now, as far as I know, it’s mostly handled manually by the instructor. If a student seems to be ignoring important feedback, the professor might follow up directly by email or in class, but I don’t believe there’s a formal automated escalation process in place today. That works okay for small classes, but it can get messy when there are many students or when the feedback is time-sensitive.

Thanks for sharing how manual follow-up is currently done. Building on that, what concerns or reservations have professors and administrators expressed about introducing automated escalation alerts? How might these concerns shape the way Virtual-EDU designs escalation and reminder features to ensure they are effective but not overwhelming or intrusive?

The biggest concern is that automated escalations could feel too invasive if they keep alerting students or staff over something minor. Professors also worry that it could create extra noise for them if they start getting notified about every unread comment instead of just the important ones. That would probably push Virtual-EDU toward clear defaults, limited escalation paths, and controls that let instructors decide what is worth chasing without turning the system into a constant reminder machine.

That makes a lot of sense, keeping escalation sensible and non-intrusive is key. Building on that, could you share how NJIT currently handles situations where students repeatedly ignore feedback notifications? Are there any manual or automated escalation steps in place today, and how effective have those been in practice?
